title: Connexions de Gauss-Manin et équations de Picard-Fuchs. Opération de Cartier : copies de tapuscrit annoté (s.d.), tiré à part (1981), notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting: P is a projective line over C. A non-empty open set D ⊂ P^an is called 'homogeneous' if its stabilizer G ⊂ Aut(P) ≅ PGL(2,C) (Grothendieck writes GP(1)_C) acts transitively on D. Transport of structure is immediate: g(D) is homogeneous with stabilizer int(g)G = gGg^{-1}.

Theorem 1 ('classical', derived from the uniformization theorem).
(a) Up to conjugation by Aut(P) there are exactly three classes of homogeneous domains:
- D = P;
- D = P minus a point (≅ C);
- an open disc.
A bracketed remark makes the third case intrinsic. Discs are taken for a PSU(2)-invariant Riemannian metric on P. Such metrics are unique up to a scalar, so the notion of open disc does not depend on the choice.
(b) The restriction map from the stabilizer G to Aut^an(D) is an isomorphism, and D is connected and simply connected.
(c) The functor (P, D) ↦ D is an equivalence of groupoids (categories 'pour iso'). The source is pairs (projective line, homogeneous domain); the target is connected, simply connected, non-singular 1-dimensional complex-analytic spaces.

Corollary: the stabilizers are
1) Aut(P) ≅ PGL(2,C);
2) Aut(E^1) ≅ Aff(1,C);
3) 'GP(1,R) ≅ GL(2,R)/R^* ≅ SL(2,R)/μ_2(R)'.
Grothendieck then contrasts cases 1 and 2, where the groups come from complex algebraic groups, with case 3, where they come from a real algebraic group.

The next page continues this. GP(1)_R is a real form of PGL_2. Real forms (descents of Aut_C P or of its Lie algebra H^0(P, T_P)) correspond to discs up to 'polarity' and to circles in P. A Scholie follows: a canonical functor X ↦ ℙ(X) with a functorial embedding X ↪ ℙ(X)(C) as a homogeneous domain.

Grothendieck then globalizes. For any non-singular curve X, the universal covers X̃(x) form a local system over the fundamental groupoid Π(X). Applying ℙ fibrewise gives a canonical flat P^1-bundle over X. It carries an integrable connection and a canonical analytic section, coming from x ↦ x̃ and the diagonal.

This is the canonical uniformizing projective structure, in modern terms the uniformization sl_2-oper. Its developing map is the uniformization. Locally it is described by the uniformizing second-order linear ODE (a Schwarzian / Fuchsian equation). That explains its place in a dossier on Gauss–Manin connections and Picard–Fuchs equations: the uniformizing equation is treated as a canonical 'Picard–Fuchs-type' connection attached to any curve.
errors: Theorem 1(a)/(b) is false for the definition as stated (open, non-empty, stabilizer acts transitively). D = C^* = P − {0,∞} is homogeneous: the stabilizer C^*⋊Z/2 acts transitively, yet D is not simply connected. So the list of three classes misses C^* and (b) fails.

Also P minus a circle (e.g. the union of the upper and lower half-planes) is homogeneous: PGL(2,R) acts transitively on it, since elements of negative determinant swap the halves. It is not connected, contradicting 'D est connexe'. The definition needs 'connected and simply connected', or must be restricted to the three domains obtained from uniformization.

Corollary case 3: the stabilizer of a disc is PSL(2,R) = SL(2,R)/μ_2. This is the identity component, of index 2, of PGL(2,R) = GL(2,R)/R^* = GP(1)(R). So the chain 'GP(1,R) ≃ GL(2,R)/R^* ≃ SL(2,R)/μ_2(R)' is wrong at the last ≃. The stabilizer of the full circle is PGL(2,R); the stabilizer of one half is PSL(2,R).
Notational slips: 'X' is used for P in (a)3° and (b). 'GP(1)' denotes PGL_2, the projective group of P^1.

ideas.what: Classification of homogeneous domains in P^1 and the equivalence between pairs (P^1, homogeneous domain) and simply connected Riemann surfaces
Automorphism groups of the three simply connected Riemann surfaces, with the remark that the disc case comes from a real form of PGL_2
ideas.modern_name: PGL(2,C), Aff(1,C), PSL(2,R) ≅ PU(1,1); real forms of PGL_2
ideas.usually_credited_to: classical (Klein, Poincaré; É. Cartan for real forms)

ideas.what: Next page: canonical functor X ↦ ℙ(X) for simply connected curves, globalized via the fundamental groupoid to a canonical flat P^1-bundle with section on any curve
ideas.modern_name: Canonical (uniformizing) projective structure; uniformization sl_2-oper; developing map; uniformizing (Fuchsian) differential equation

missed.claim: Grothendieck places the uniformizing projective structure, a canonical flat P^1-bundle with transverse section, inside a dossier on Gauss–Manin connections and Picard–Fuchs equations. He treats uniformization as a canonical connection attached to any curve. This prefigures the oper viewpoint and the comparison between uniformizing equations and Picard–Fuchs equations, e.g. for modular curves.
missed.quote: Le "théorème d'uniformisation" nous donne ... Th. (classique) 1 ... c) Le foncteur (P, D) ↦ D ... est une équivalence de catégories.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Mainly historical: it documents that Grothendieck thought about uniformization functorially, via groupoids and connections, in the 1970s, before opers became standard. The mathematics itself is classical.

deep.surprise_reason: The content is classical uniformization in a careful categorical/groupoid packaging, containing small errors (missing C^* and P minus a circle; PGL(2,R) vs PSL(2,R)). The mild interest lies in the continuation: a canonical flat projective bundle on any curve, framed alongside Gauss–Manin/Picard–Fuchs, anticipating the oper viewpoint. This is known in substance (Poincaré, Gunning).
transcription_corrections: 'GP(1)_C' / 'GP(1,C)' should be read as Grothendieck's notation for PGL(2), the projective group of P^1.
'sur X' in (a)3° and 'dans X' in (b) are Grothendieck's slips for P, as visible in the image.
In corollary 3), the image reads 'GP(1,R) ≃ Gl(2,R)/R^* ≃ Sl(2,R)/μ_2(R)'; the transcription is consistent with that.
